knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 52-year-old Spanish-speaking male presented to the hospital with a two-month history of a 40-lb weight loss and occasional diarrhea. He had previously visited his primary care provider multiple times before being referred to the emergency department (ED). The patient was admitted due to his weight loss, shortness of breath with exertion, fatigue, and malaise. He also reported recurrent nausea with nonbilious vomiting, loose stools, and 'brown' urine. His social history indicated no smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use. He works as a truck driver and is married with two adult children. His medical history includes gout, for which he takes allopurinol, with no other known conditions or previous hospitalizations or surgeries. In the ED, his vital signs were: temperature 36.9°C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 158/48 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98%. The initial physical examination was normal, with no gross lesions, excoriations, or hemorrhaging; cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and musculoskeletal exams were unremarkable. knowledge_fragments.content:
Nausea is the sensation of impending emesis and is frequently accompanied by autonomic changes,

such as increased heart rate and salivation. Nausea and vomiting typically occur in sequence; however,

they can occur separately (eg, vomiting can occur without preceding nausea as a result of increased

intracranial pressure).

Vomiting is uncomfortable and can cause dehydration because fluid is lost and because the ability to

rehydrate by drinking is limited.
knowledge_fragments.title: Chapter 268. Approach to the Care of Normal Infants & Children > Nausea and Vomiting > Introduction

knowledge_fragments.content:
(For nausea and vomiting in infants and children, see p.

.)

Nausea, the unpleasant feeling of needing to vomit, represents awareness of afferent stimuli (including

increased parasympathetic tone) to the medullary vomiting center. Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of

gastric contents caused by involuntary contraction of the abdominal musculature when the gastric fundus

and lower esophageal sphincter are relaxed.

Vomiting should be distinguished from regurgitation, the spitting up of gastric contents without associated

nausea or forceful abdominal muscular contractions. Patients with achalasia or a Zenker's diverticulum

may regurgitate undigested food without nausea.
knowledge_fragments.title: Chapter 7. Approach to the Patient With Upper GI Complaints > Nausea and Vomiting > Introduction

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Histoplasmosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis. The biopsy revealed an ulcer base with fungus (spores with some budding).. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 52-year-old Spanish-speaking male presented to the hospital with a two-month history of a 40-lb weight loss and occasional diarrhea. He had previously visited his primary care provider multiple times before being referred to the emergency department (ED). The patient was admitted due to his weight loss, shortness of breath with exertion, fatigue, and malaise. He also reported recurrent nausea with nonbilious vomiting, loose stools, and 'brown' urine. His social history indicated no smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use. He works as a truck driver and is married with two adult children. His medical history includes gout, for which he takes allopurinol, with no other known conditions or previous hospitalizations or surgeries. In the ED, his vital signs were: temperature 36.9°C, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 158/48 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98%. knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Histoplasmosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis. The biopsy revealed an ulcer base with fungus (spores with some budding).. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.

knowledge_fragments.content:
Nausea is the sensation of impending emesis and is frequently accompanied by autonomic changes,

such as increased heart rate and salivation. Nausea and vomiting typically occur in sequence; however,

they can occur separately (eg, vomiting can occur without preceding nausea as a result of increased

intracranial pressure).

Vomiting is uncomfortable and can cause dehydration because fluid is lost and because the ability to

rehydrate by drinking is limited.

tree.case_summary:
A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with nausea and vomiting for the past week. He decided to come in when his symptoms worsened. He feels that his symptoms are exacerbated with large fatty meals and when he drinks alcohol. His wife recently returned from a cruise with symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea. The patient has a medical history of poorly managed diabetes, constipation, anxiety, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 197/128 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam reveals a systolic murmur heard loudest along the left upper sternal border. Abdominal exam reveals an obese, tympanitic and distended abdomen with a 3 cm scar in the right lower quadrant. Vascular exam reveals weak pulses in the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's symptoms?

Options:
A. Adhesions
B. Enteric nervous system damage
C. Impacted stool
D. Norovirus
E. Twisting of the bowel

alarm_features: weak pulses in the lower extremities
excluded_candidates: Gastroesophageal reflux disease: less likely due to absence of typical symptoms such as heartburn
Inflammatory bowel disease: less likely due to absence of typical symptoms such as diarrhea and abdominal pain
Viral gastroenteritis: possible but less likely due to the subacute nature of the symptoms and the absence of diarrhea in the patient
